analysis.one_liner: Imposes fiduciary duties on mortgage servicers, bans dual-tracking foreclosures, and requires principal forgiveness.
analysis.headline: Introduced in May 2011 with bipartisan cosponsorship, the bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill responds to the robo-signing and foreclosure abuses that followed the housing crash. It would make mortgage servicers — the companies that collect homeowners' payments and handle defaults — act as fiduciaries for the investors who own the loans, bar them from foreclosing while a borrower is being evaluated for an affordable loan modification, require principal forgiveness for underwater homeowners when the numbers favor it, cap foreclosure-related fees at cost, and stop servicers from collecting improper fees or charging inflated force-placed insurance. Homeowners would get new rights to sue, and a foreclosure could be blocked outright if the servicer broke the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners facing foreclosure or struggling with a securitized mortgage, who would gain a single point of contact, protection from dual-tracking, documented proof of the right to foreclose, and earned principal forgiveness; also investors in mortgage-backed securities, who would gain a servicer fiduciary duty and easier trustee removal.

how_it_helps.text: Servicers could not start or continue a foreclosure while deciding whether the borrower qualifies for an affordable loan modification, and failing to follow the rules would be a legal bar to the foreclosure itself [S3].

Servicers would have to offer earned principal forgiveness up to the maximum amount with a positive net present value, forgiven in thirds over three years, to bring payments to an affordable level [S3].

Servicers of mortgage-backed securities would owe a non-waivable fiduciary duty to investors, could not commingle homeowners' payments with their own assets, and could be removed by a petition of 50% of investors [S2] [S3].

All settlement and servicing fees would have to be reasonably related to the cost of the service, servicers could not route the work through their own subsidiaries to mark it up, and force-placed insurance would have to cost and cover about the same as a standard homeowner policy [S3].

A servicer committing unfair or deceptive practices could owe up to $10,000 per violation plus actual damages including emotional distress and attorneys' fees, and foreclosure debt collection would fall under the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage servicers and their bank affiliates, which would face fiduciary duties, fee caps, a prohibition on owning competing liens on the same property, independent capital reserve requirements, executive clawbacks tied to securities fraud convictions, and heavy per-violation liability; force-placed insurers would lose inflated premium business.

drawbacks.text: The bill forecloses only after a documented eligibility determination and requires servicers to hand over notes, assignments, and pooling agreements before foreclosing, which critics said would slow legitimate foreclosures and could discourage securitized lending going forward [S3].

Earned principal forgiveness would write down loan balances, reducing recoveries for mortgage-backed security investors, including pension funds and other holders, even though the bill calculates relief across all investor classes [S3].
The ban on servicers or affiliates holding any interest in another mortgage on the same property would have forced major restructuring of the second-lien and servicing businesses of large banks [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections were substantial and directly aimed at documented foreclosure abuses: dual-tracking, robo-signed documents, inflated force-placed insurance, and improper fees. The costs fall almost entirely on servicers and banks rather than on other borrowers, though tighter foreclosure standards and forced principal write-downs would have reduced investor recoveries and could have added friction to the mortgage market. On balance the benefits to distressed homeowners outweighed the compliance costs, but the bill also carried broad new mandates whose implementation burden would have been significant for the industry.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Brad Miller (D-NC) introduced the bill on May 5, 2011, with Reps. George Miller (D-CA), Michael Turner (R-OH), John Conyers (D-MI), and Al Green (D-TX) as original cosponsors [S1] [S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services on the day of introduction and the record shows no further action of any kind for the remainder of the 112th Congress [S5].
The bill attracted six cosponsors, five Democrats and one Republican [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage servicers and their bank affiliates kept operating under the pre-existing rules, with no fiduciary duty, no foreclosure bars, and no new liability, while homeowners in foreclosure received none of the bill's protections.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship was nominally bipartisan — five Democrats and one Republican cosponsor — but no vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape of the chamber on the bill was never measured.

industries.industry: Mortgage servicers and their bank affiliates
industries.note: The bill's core targets: a non-waivable fiduciary duty to investors, a ban on commingling homeowners' payments, cost-based fee caps, a ban on holding competing liens on the same property, executive clawbacks for securities fraud, and up to $10,000 per violation in damages with a bar to foreclosure for violations. Servicers profited from foreclosure-related fees, force-placed insurance kickbacks, and dual-tracking, all of which the bill would have ended.

Force-placed policies often cost far more than standard homeowner coverage, with commissions flowing back to servicers; the bill would have required cost and coverage substantially equivalent to a standard policy and let servicers keep or reinstate the borrower's own policy instead.

Servicers would owe investors a fiduciary duty, trustees would have to verify statements, delinquent loans would be marked to market, and investors could petition courts to remove trustee-servicers or amend pooling agreements — protections absent after the crisis. Investors include pensions and mutual funds alongside large financial institutions.
